sheet.name: Brakka Ironvein
sheet.opening: Brakka Ironvein served six years as a guard at the Temple of the Anvil Father in Greyhollow, a mining town cut into a cold mountainside. Three days ago three miners went down into the old north workings, which were sealed a generation ago, and none came back. Last night a fourth man came up out of the dark alone, babbling about lights that walk, then died before dawn. The town council will brick up the mine entrance at sunrise tomorrow, missing miners or not. The temple's prior, an old dwarf named Hessa, has asked Brakka to go down before then and bring back whoever can still be brought back. It is late afternoon, and Brakka stands at the mine mouth with a lantern borrowed from the temple.

transcript.text: notebook: created an entry for Recovering the miners; added 2 relationships to Recovering the miners

Greyhollow is a mean little town with a rich vein under it: houses of dark stone huddled against a mountainside where winter lingers long past its season. The Anvil Father — god of forgework, patience, and iron that holds — has a temple here, and for six years you, Brakka Ironvein, kept its gate. Not the loftiest calling for a dwarf of the Ironveins, but steady, and the prior trusted you.

Three days ago, three miners pried open the old north workings — sealed a generation back, before your time — and went down. None came up. Last night a fourth man crawled out alone, raving about lights that walk in the dark, and died before dawn with cold in his bones. The council has had enough: at sunrise, masons brick the entrance shut, souls inside or no souls at all.

Hessa, the temple's prior, put her old hand on your shoulder this morning. "Bring back whoever can still be brought back," she said, and lent you a hooded lantern. That is all the send-off you got.

Now it is late afternoon, the light going grey and cold, and you stand at the mine mouth. The new timber around the old seal is splintered where the miners broke through, and beyond it the shaft breathes out cold air that smells of wet stone and something faintly wrong underneath, like snuffed candles. Your lantern is unlit at your hip. The descent ahead is dark, and sunrise is your deadline.

What does Brakka do?

I light the hooded lantern and check my gear before going in: shield on my arm, weapon loose in its sheath. Then I crouch at the splintered timbers to look for tracks or dropped tools from the three miners before I step through.

The lantern catches on the first try, its flame steadying behind smudged glass, half-shielded by the hood. You set it between your boots while you work: buckles of the shield strap cinched, the longsword drawn a hand's width and slid back — loose, the way you like it. Crossbow slung. Rope on your hip. All as it should be.

The ground at the entrance is another matter. The cold has baked the trampled mud into a hard crust, and between that, your own six years of tramping gate duty, and the dark closing in, you can make little of it. You can see that boots went in — that much is obvious from the splintered seal — but how many, how fast, whether they came back out at any point, whether anything followed the fourth man up... the earth won't say. You're no tracker.

One thing does catch the lantern light, tucked against the inside of the new timber where someone must have set it down and never picked it up: a short-handled miner's pick, and beside it a horn whistle on a thong, the kind the miners carry to signal along the levels.

Cold air moves past your face, up out of the shaft, steady as breathing. Somewhere below, faint, you think you hear stone knock against stone — once, twice — like a hammer on the Anvil Father's forge. Or like water. Or like nothing.

Beyond the broken seal, a rough stair of cut steps descends into the dark, slick with old damp.

Your lantern will burn about six hours on its oil. It's near a quarter to six in the evening; sunrise is your wall.

What does Brakka do?

I pocket the horn whistle on its thong, since it might let me signal the miners or be a way to be heard in the dark. Then I pick up the lantern and descend the cut steps slowly, shield forward, testing each wet step with my boot and listening for that knocking sound.

You slip the horn whistle over your neck beside the holy symbol and take up the lantern.

The first steps are the worst for slip, but dwarves are born to stone, and you take them slow, boot-heel first. The stair runs down deeper than any worked level you know of in Greyhollow — fifty steps, then a turn in the rock, then fifty more, the lantern's hooded beam swinging shadows across walls scored with pick-marks a generation old.

Halfway down, you stop. And this time you hear it, truly hear it: not water, not loose rock. It's knocking — metal on stone, coming up from below and to the east. And it's in a pattern. Three knocks, a pause, then three more. Three-and-three, over and over, patient as a heartbeat.

You know that pattern. Every tunnel-child of Greyhollow knows the miners' tapping code. Three-and-three is the oldest signal in it: alive, alive, still alive. Someone down there is awake, and hammering for anyone who might hear.

That's more than you hoped for an hour ago. But a cold thought follows it: whoever is knocking never knocked when the fourth man climbed out past them — or he did, and the man who died didn't care to answer.

At the stair's foot the passage opens onto a landing where the mud is churned by many boots — too jumbled for you to count sets or say which way any man walked, and you are no tracker. The best you can say is that bodies went both ways through here, and one line of prints looks dragged and stumbling, as if made by a man barely walking. Between you and the knocking, a tunnel runs east, and the lantern light catches an old mine cart half off its rails, a rake of rusted tools, and a timber post chalked with a paw-shaped smear of old paint. Past the cart, something pale and small lies on the floor of the tunnel.

What does Brakka do?

I use the whistle's thong as a reminder to stay quiet and don't answer yet; I want to know what I'm walking into first. I advance east along the tunnel, shield up and lantern low, and stop at the cart to check the pale thing on the floor from a few paces before I touch it.
dice Brakka's Perception check scanning the tunnel by the cart (lantern light): 1d20+4 (advantage) = 1d20 [1, 5]→5 + 4 = 9

You leave the whistle hanging silent and move east, unhurried, keeping your weight on your boot heels. The tunnel swallows the last daylight behind you; the lantern's shielded beam is your whole world now.

You stop two paces short of the pale thing. It lies near the cart's ruined wheel, and you lean the lantern low over it without going closer.

It's a candle. A stub of pale tallow, no longer than your thumb, burned hollow at the wick, set upright on the stone as carefully as if someone placed it there. The flame is long gone. What keeps the small hairs up on your neck is the spiral of soot around the stub — the wax burned while standing here, down near floor level, far out of anyone's reach of the entrance, with no holder, no sconce, no smear of drips on the wall above it. A candle that simply sat on bare rock and burned itself down. Carved into its base, faint and worn, is a little struck anvil — maker's mark or god's sign, you can't say. The Anvil Father's mark would be warm to your touch, temple work being yours. This one isn't. This one feels like something copied from his sign by someone who'd only had it described.

You kneel there, hurry-thumping heart and steady hand. The knocking goes on eastward, three-and-three, patient as water — and you notice that when your boots scuffed the gravel by the cart, the knocking stopped a moment after, listening, going still as stone before it started again. Whatever hammers will have heard you coming. It waits for an answer, and waits — three and three, still alive. Honest men answer that call, sooner or later. But you've been a gate-guard long enough to know that other things knock, too.

Down the tunnel east, the lantern shows maybe forty feet before the dark swallows it, timber crosses marching away like ribs.

What does Brakka do?

I leave the candle where it lies, but I press my holy symbol in my fist and whisper a short prayer to the Anvil Father before moving on. Then I creep east along the timbers, shield up and lantern shuttered down to a sliver, stopping every ten paces to listen for the knocking and anything moving behind it.

You press the anvil to your lips and murmur the short prayer — iron that holds, Father, hold me — and go on with the lantern shuttered to a knife of light.

It's slow going, and the chain mail works against you, but you move the way you learned on night gate: boot finding stone before weight follows, breath low, no metal allowed to touch metal. Whatever listens down here, you'll not give it your footsteps cheap.

The knocking draws you east, then bends north at a junction where the timber is older and splintered — and there, thirty paces on, a side gallery mouths open, half-choked with a fall of rubble. The knocking comes from behind the fall. As your light gropes up to it, the hammering stutters and stops. A cough. Then a voice, cracked and small, from between two boulders where a gap shows dark: "Is someone there? By the Father, quickly — the candle — don't let them light me —"

Through the gap, lanternlight on a smutched face and one terrified eye. A living miner, sitting wedged in the rubble with one leg pinned under a slab, a pick-head in his fist — the hammer you heard. He's been down here three days on cold drip-water and whatever chalk he could scrape off the wall. He whispers his name like a prayer: Doran.

"Don't answer them," he breathes, eyes rolling toward the main tunnel behind you. "They knock back. They knock perfect, like a man, but they knock too patient. That's how they got Garl. And Fenn near the shaft — a little light took him, soft as a candle coming, and he went to it smiling."

Far down the main tunnel, south and behind you, at the very edge of the shuttered lantern's reach — two small pale lights hang in the black. Not lanterns. They sway gently, side to side, the way a lamp swings in a walker's hand. They are not coming closer. They are waiting, patient as you were told.

Doran's hand gropes through the gap for you, and beyond, the rubble fall rises halfway to the ceiling, sloped and shifty-looking, three tons of bad masonry between your hands and his.

What does Brakka do?

I whisper to Doran, "Stay quiet, friend, I'm Brakka from the temple gate. I'm getting you out." I take his hand briefly, then shutter the lantern fully and ask in a low voice, "Doran, what do the lights fear? Does your pick-hammer or any iron or the Father's holy symbol keep them off?"

You grip Doran's hand through the gap — his fingers are ice-cold and shaking, but they close on yours like a smith's vice. "Brakka," he whispers back, half-laughing with relief, "the Anvil Father sends me a gate-guard."

You close the lantern's shutter entirely, and darkness folds down over the both of you like a lid. Somewhere far south, the pale lights still hang. Doubling your night-sight in this velvet black, you can just make them out — unchanged, patient.

"Keep it dark," Doran breathes, "they come to light when it's small. A candle, a guttering torch — small light draws 'em, like moths if moths hunted men. Garl's lamp died and they came for him within the hour. And when I threw Fenn a burning rag off a stick, they swung off wide around its flare — bright light they'll skirt, and small light they'll stalk toward."

"Your iron and your sign?" A bitter, cracked whisper. "Fenn had the anvil burned into his pick-haft, same as mine. Didn't slow them. They're not wolves to be fought, Brakka. They knock like men and they light like candles and they wait. They waited three days for me. They want me to walk to them."

In the blackness, the pale lights shift for the first time — they've drifted a slow, lazy ten feet closer along the main tunnel, in perfect silence, and stopped again. They're at the edge of where your own darkness ends, patient as you were told, waiting for the moment the small light they love comes back.

You know darkness yourself — sixty feet of it, grey but seeing, yours without any flame at all.

What does Brakka do?

I whisper, "Easy, Doran. I see in the dark, so I don't need the lantern at all." I keep the lantern shuttered and go to work on the rubble, shifting the slab off his leg first, lifting with my legs and bracing my shield arm, careful to make as little noise as I can. I keep one eye on those two pale lights while I do it.

RULE Combat Step by Step:
1.  **Determine surprise.** The GM determines whether anyone involved in the combat encounter is surprised.
2.  **Establish positions.** The GM decides where all the characters and monsters are located. Given the adventurers' marching order or their stated positions in the room or other location, the GM figures out where the adversaries are/how far away and in what direction.
3.  **Roll initiative.** Everyone involved in the combat encounter rolls initiative, determining the order of combatants' turns.
4.  **Take turns.** Each participant in the battle takes a turn in initiative order.
5.  **Begin the next round.** When everyone involved in the combat has had a turn, the round ends. Repeat step 4 until the fighting stops.

The rules sections these steps name, in full:

RULE Surprise:
A band of adventurers sneaks up on a bandit camp, springing from the trees to attack them. A gelatinous cube glides down a dungeon passage, unnoticed by the adventurers until the cube engulfs one of them. In these situations, one side of the battle gains surprise over the other.

The GM determines who might be surprised. If neither side tries to be stealthy, they automatically notice each other. Otherwise, the GM compares the Dexterity (Stealth) checks of anyone hiding with the passive Wisdom (Perception) score of each creature on the opposing side. Any character or monster that doesn't notice a threat is surprised at the start of the encounter.

If you're surprised, you can't move or take an action on your first turn of the combat, and you can't take a reaction until that turn ends. A member of a group can be surprised even if the other members aren't.

RULE The Order of Combat:
A typical combat encounter is a clash between two sides, a flurry of weapon swings, feints, parries, footwork, and spellcasting. The game organizes the chaos of combat into a cycle of rounds and turns. A **round** represents about 6 seconds in the game world. During a round, each participant in a battle takes a **turn**. The order of turns is determined at the beginning of a combat encounter, when everyone rolls initiative. Once everyone has taken a turn, the fight continues to the next round if neither side has defeated the other.

Sections inside it (look each up): Combat Step by Step, Surprise, Initiative, Your Turn, Reactions

RULE Initiative:
Initiative determines the order of turns during combat. When combat starts, every participant makes a Dexterity check to determine their place in the initiative order. The GM makes one roll for an entire group of identical creatures, so each member of the group acts at the same time.

The GM ranks the combatants in order from the one with the highest Dexterity check total to the one with the lowest. This is the order (called the initiative order) in which they act during each round. The initiative order remains the same from round to round.

If a tie occurs, the GM decides the order among tied GM-controlled creatures, and the players decide the order among their tied characters. The GM can decide the order if the tie is between a monster and a player character. Optionally, the GM can have the tied characters and monsters each roll a d20 to determine the order, highest roll going first.

The light closes on you fast — like a lamp swinging in a sprinting man's hand — and stops dead a foot from your shield-face, swelling from candle-glow to bonfire-bright in the space of a heartbeat. For half a blink, and only that, you can see inside it: a little curling blue-white shape, like a knot of pale smoke, hovering.

Then it strikes. Lightning leaps the small gap and slams through your shield arm and armor both, every joint in your body locking at once, your teeth buzzing. Your chain mail rings like a struck bell. You've taken worse knocks from the forge-gang's brawls, but not many — the pain sits in your bones and stays. You're standing, barely rocked, at 5 of your full strength out of 14; your breath is ragged.

The walker hangs there at the rim of your shield, bright and patient, like a smith waiting to see if the iron's done.

Behind you, Doran keeps flat behind the rubble as you ordered, but his voice carries a hiss of pure terror across the gap: "When it swells bright, it's striking! Bright means strike — and there's two of them, remember! TWO!"

Your turn, Brakka.

I'm hurt badly, but I stay planted and swing my longsword at the walker, then try to keep it pinned against my shield so it can't dart around me to Doran. If I drop low, I'll use Second Wind first: DM, I'll use my bonus action to Second Wind, then attack.

You are not there for most of it, Brakka. You'll have it from Doran's mouth later, hoarse and wondering, and this is how he'll tell it:

How he planted one torch upright in a crack of the rubble so the dark couldn't sneak in behind you, and hauled you by the collar, one fist of fire sweeping, fifteen feet at a time, while the walker circled at the rim of the light like a wolf pacing a fire ring. How he heard the water of your breathing change as he dragged you over the landing stones, and knew you were holding on. How at the stair's foot he rammed both torches together into one blazing bloom and swung you over his shoulder — a dwarf in chain mail, heavier than any ore-cart — and climbed, one step at a time, a hundred wet steps of the ancestors, weeping and swearing in the same breath, while the pale light swelled below him in a fury it could not spend.

And how, at the top, he set you down on cold grass under real stars, took the horn whistle from around your neck, and blew three-and-three into the night until his lungs tore — alive, alive, still alive — while behind the two of you, out of the broken seal, the mine breathed its cold, and somewhere down in it a light hung patient, and another one hung farther off, waiting for easier men.

They came — townsfolk, masons, Hessa herself with her robes kilted up and a lantern in her fist, running through the dusk on the strength of that whistle. You'll wake to her voice, near midnight, in a bed under the temple's roof, with every ache in your body speaking at once but your heart still beating — you pulled through the night on your own iron, Brakka, waking at last with a thread of your strength back. Doran is on the next cot, swaddled and fed, telling anyone who'll listen that the gate-guard came down and stood between him and the dark.

For that — going down before sunrise and bringing back the one soul that could be brought back — the night pays you its dues (225 XP toward your next level; 225 of 300).

But morning is coming, and this is what you know before any councilman does: the mine mouth is to be bricked at sunrise regardless, with Brakka in it or not — and down in the dark, the walking lights are still waiting, and Garl and Fenn are down there still. They knocked like men, once. Perfect. Too patient.

What does Brakka do, waking in the temple infirmary near midnight?

I sit up slowly, wincing, and find Hessa. "Prior, thank the Father. Don't let the masons brick that entrance at dawn: the lights hold Garl and Fenn down there, and iron can't touch them, but fire drives them off." I ask Doran quietly from the next cot what else he knows about them, and whether he'd say anything to the council himself, since he's the one living witness.

Hessa is in the chair beside your cot, prayer book open on her knees, and hasn't left it, they say. She hears you out — the walker, the lightning, the treadmill of dark — without one flicker of surprise, which surprises you.

"So it was them," she says at last, very quietly. "I had a whole homily prepared to convince you not to go down, and the Father spared me the waste." She looks at you a long moment. "The council will brick it at dawn either way, Brakka; they're frightened men, and frightened men like finished walls. But hear this from me, as one of the temple: iron and the anvil mark mean nothing to those things — you've the bruises to prove it — but there is old work beneath that seal. In Doran's grandfather's day, miners went down the north workings and didn't come up, and the temple of that generation didn't fight what they found. The prior of those days sealed the workings with prayer and left candle offerings at the mouth — a rite even I only half remember. Whatever walked then was bottled, not slain. Your friend with the torch bought back its patience, and that's the whole of our victory today."

At your question, Doran drags himself onto one elbow from the next cot, grey-faced but sharp-eyed. "Testify? Aye, if you hold my arm up in front of me." His voice steadies as an idea takes him. "Give me one hour at that council with a torch in my fist and they'll not lay one brick till they've heard every cracked word from me. But they like walls, the council." He looks sideways at you, then says the thing that's been sitting behind his eyes:

"Brakka. My grandfather sealed that drift. But he told me once, drunk and honest: 'The wall's the third wall down there. The first two our fathers built, and the Lights came through both.' Three walls. That's what he said. There's something down beneath the north workings that even the lights answer to."

Hessa stands. "Rest tonight, both of you, or I'll have the cots nailed shut. Before dawn, if anyone moves that council, it'll be these three: Doran's tongue, my prior's oath, or your hands, gate-guard. Sleep and choose."

It is near midnight. Sunrise is roughly six hours off. Fire, walls old and new, and something below that even the lights answer to. What does Brakka do?

I settle back on the cot but don't sleep yet. "Prior, you said the old rite left candle offerings at the mouth. Do you remember any of it, or is there a record in the temple archive? I'd like to see it before dawn, and the candle I found down there with the false anvil mark might matter, so I'll tell you about it."

Then I turn to Doran. "Rest, friend. At first light, you and Hessa go to the council, and I'll stand behind you in my armor so they see the temple means it."

Hessa takes you down the archive stair herself, lamplight on stone shelves, and you tell her of the candle on your way — the pale stub, the copied anvil, burned hollow standing on bare rock with no hand near it. She stops on the stair at that, and her face does flicker now.

"Then the seal's been nursed at," she says. "Someone set the door open a crack."

The search is long — you are no scholar, and your head still rings — but dwarves read stone-quiet rooms well, and somewhere past midnight your hand finds what the temple's own memory lost: the prior's record of the sealing, in her own crabbed hand. The rite is called the Vigil of Bottled Dark. Tallow candles stamped with the anvil — the mark struck and blessed by temple hands, temple hands, it says twice, underscored — set burning at the mouth at dusk, every equinox, one generation of quiet keeping on another. The wall never held the lights, and neither did iron, as Hessa told you; but a mark struck and blessed by temple hands, and burned, is another matter. The ward was never the wall. The ward was the true flame.

And then the page that makes sense of your candle at the mine: a warning, in the same crabbed hand. A false mark — an anvil copied by hands outside the temple — does not ward. It invites. Such candles are found burning on bare stone in the dark, unwitnessed, small flames the lights carry in front of them like lanterns held out. And beneath the warning, a note: false-mark candles were found once before, in the workings, in the year of the second wall. The miners who'd carried them down could not say who'd taught them the making — only that a peddler had come through Greyhollow shortly before men began going down and not coming up. The page calls what waits below the third wall nothing but a name half-ashamed of itself: the cold tallow.

Hessa reads the page twice, then sits down on the archive stair like her knees have been unhinged. "The equinox rites were kept in my grandmother's time," she says slowly. "I thought them a dead grandmother's superstition. In mine, the archive says, they were missed — twice. And someone has been selling false candles to our miners." Her jaw sets like cooling steel. "There is tallow in this temple, and there is a true anvil-seal stamp in my own keeping. If the council wants a wall at dawn, then they'll get a warded wall, by the Father, with true flame at its mouth, or I'll know the reason."

Doran is already asleep on his cot when you pass through, one arm hung down toward the floor. It is near half past midnight. Sunrise, the council, the masons, Doran's testimony, a peddler somewhere in Greyhollow's memory — and perhaps six hours of sleep, or fewer. What does Brakka do?

I tell Hessa, "Then let's make the true candles tonight. Show me the stamp and the tallow, and I'll help you pour and strike them before dawn, since I'll be standing at that wall anyway." While we work, I ask her whether anyone in town has bought or sold tallow lately, or if she remembers any peddler passing through Greyhollow in the last season or two.

The back room of the temple smells of rendered fat and herbs until dawn comes up grey. Hessa strikes the anvil-seal into each candle's base herself — temple hands, she says again, like a smith saying good iron — while you stir the tallow, pour the molds, and set each finished stub on waxed cloth. Twelve true candles before the birds start. Your own hands know the work; turns out a gate-guard who six years watched the forge-priests at their bench remembers more than he thought. You don't sleep, and by the last hour your body's telling you so — you are still at a thread of your strength, and your breath is long, unwound iron. (You'll feel this until you truly rest, Brakka.)

On the peddler, she can give you this much, stirring beside you: a tinker with a cart — no name anyone kept — came through Greyhollow a month or so back, round the winter market, selling cheap candles in lots to the miners' rows. "Cheap tallow, pale wax, no temple stamp on any of them, and the miners bought them by the dozen because winter nights are long." She can't swear it's the trade the old prior wrote of. But she says the timing sits with her like a bad tooth.

At first light you carry the crate to the mine mouth together, Doran hobbling at your side wrapped in the temple's grey, and the mountain shows you what the council means by finished walls: two masons and a handcart of bricks already waiting, breath steaming, and behind them half of Greyhollow — the council in their cloaks, miners' families, children on shoulders. Cold morning fog lies in the cut like milk.

The council head — a heavy woman named Brama, quarrymistress — looks from Hessa to the crate of candles to the wall of the hill. "Prior," she says carefully, "the town slept badly. Say what you've come to say."

It's near half five in the morning. The crowd is listening, Doran is squaring his shoulders to speak, and the sun is climbing.

What does Brakka do?

I step up beside Hessa in my armor, shield on my arm so the crowd sees the temple means it, and say in a voice that carries, "Quarrymistress Brama, I went down there and came back with Doran. The lights are real, and iron won't touch them. Let the prior and Doran speak, and let the wall go up with true candles burning at its mouth, as the old Vigil of Bottled Dark commands."

Then I add, "And ask the miners' rows who bought those cheap pale candles from the tinker's cart last month. Garl and Fenn may still be down there, and the false ones are what drew the lights."

You say your piece, and the mountain gives you back a fine echo — but echoes don't persuade. You're a gate-guard, not a town-meeting man, and the words come out too proud, too much like a soldier telling quarrymen their business. Brama's jaw sets; you can see it going wrong in real time. When Doran tries after you, his cracked voice fails in the wind, and the crowd's murmur turns against you both — too much dark talk before breakfast, too much 问 the council doesn't want.

Brama's answer comes flat as a tomb lid. "The wall goes up this morning, and no more men go behind it. Garl and Fenn are two nights dead by any sane count, and I won't feed this town a third ghost story." She looks at the crate of candles, though, and at Hessa's face, and gives ground exactly once, a quarrymistress's one clean concession: "Set your fires, Prior, if the temple wants them. But the bricks come after."

And that is how it's done. The sun clears the ridge while Hessa lights the first of the twelve at the mouth, striking the blessing on each — temple hands, the old words, low and tarry and sincere — and the masons' mortar starts singing behind her. Doran stands with his hand on your shoulder and doesn't look away. The Vigil holds again as of this sunrise: true flame at the mouth, the wall behind it, the lights bottled in the dark with Garl and Fenn's bones.

You kept the whole of what Hessa asked, Brakka — you brought back the one who could be brought back. The two below are beyond any hand now; even Doran says it quietly, at last. The quest the prior gave you is finished.

But there's a thread left trailing out of the crowd. As the families disperse, a small woman with a miner's dead husband's ring on a cord — Garl's wife — stops in front of you. "Tinker with a cart, aye. Grey-gloved hands, that one. Paid in coin, never haggled on a candle, always in lots. Went west on the high road when he left." She looks at you with eyes that have decided about their own grief already. "He'll come back, or come to some other town. Someone set our door open, gate-guard. Find him."

You're empty, Brakka — every hour of the night spent on your feet, strength still at one thread. The temple has a cot with your name on it, and real sleep, and the Father knows you've earned it. What do you do?

I nod to Garl's wife. "I'll find him. You have my word, and I'll carry it as far as the high road goes." Then I ask her gently for her name, and whether Garl kept any of those candles he bought, before I go back to the temple to sleep.

"Nel," she says. "Nel, wife of Garl三十年 — thirty years we had the same roof and one roof more didn't come." She fetches the answer to your question from a pocket, and it's worse than you hoped and better than it could have been: one candle stub, pale and cheap, found in Garl's coat pocket when they brought his kit home. You turn it in your fingers. There in the base, faint and wrong, is an anvil copy — the same false mark you saw burned hollow on bare rock at the bottom of the dark. She presses it into your hand and won't take it back. "He carried a piece of the thing that took him home in his own pocket," she says, steady as a quarry wall. "You keep it, so you know what you're hunting. West on the high road, grey gloves, never haggle. I'll not bury a third man, gate-guard. Go."

From Hessa: yes to the lantern — she has the temple boy refill its oil, and it stays with you till you come back. Eight of the twelve true candles are left, stored in the temple's cool room and at your disposition; four burn with the old words at the warded mouth. Take what you need when you go.

And then you sleep — the real thing at last, on the infirmary cot, through the morning and past it, dreamless as forged iron. When you open your eyes the light through the shutters says afternoon, near half past two, and your body is yours again: strength full at fourteen, wind and wits restored, the night's bruises gone down to aches and the beautiful creak of a working frame. Doran has been up since noon, fed and walking on his own; the masons finished the wall at midday, mortar drying, the true flames standing their watch.

You have your word to keep, Brakka: the high road west, grey gloves, a cart, and the stub in your pocket. What does Brakka do?

I gear up, strap on my shield, and pack four of the true candles along with the lantern and the false stub from Garl's pocket. Before I leave I find Doran and Hessa: "Doran, if you remember anything about that tinker, even a cart color or a mule's name, tell me now. Prior, any word I should carry to the villages west?"

Then I'll head out onto the high road and ask at the first farm or toll post whether a grey-gloved tinker passed through.

Doron — Doran — doesn't have much, and he's honest about it. He never bought from the tinker himself; Garl did the buying for their crew. But he screws his eyes shut and comes up with two things: the tinker never once took his gloves off, not to count coins, not in the cold and not out of it. And the cart was grey too — grey wood, grey canvas, a handcart, no mule at all. A man who pulls his own cart for a living has legs and lungs; Doran says he remembers thinking the tinker's weren't right. "Too settled, like he's not working at it."

Hessa gives you her word to carry west, and it's a heavy one to hand a door-to-door errand: warn the villages' temple folk to look in their own archives — any town that ever sealed a dark place with a rite and then forgot it is a town with a door a stranger learned to knock on. "And Brakka," she adds, at the temple door, in the tone she used to use on his first year at the gate, "iron and marks and walls have all failed once in living memory what kindness and honest flaming tallow mended. Bring both."

You walk. The high road west runs downgrade out of the cold, through firs and then thin farms, the afternoon going long and amber, your strength back in your legs for the first time in two days. At the first hard-beaten farm they shake their heads at the tinker. At the second, a woman washing in the yard remembers grey gloves, but not when.

The answer comes at Copper Ford, at dusk, where the road crosses the river on a stone bridge with a toll-booth — an old man with a brazier and time to talk, who gives his name as Odo. He lights up at the description. "Tinker, grey gloves, handcart full of candles, three weeks back and more. Paid the toll in old coin and never haggled." He turns your description over, and adds the thing that's worth the whole day's walk: "Asked me, friendly as bread, which villages on this road had mines in 'em. I told him truth — Copper Ford's got pits, and past us, the quarry towns by Slatewick, further west, all dug into the hills. He nodded like a man ticking a list."

Slatewick, then, past the quarry towns, west. Copper Ford has an inn with a fire going, hot food, and beds; the light is nearly gone. What does Brakka do?

I thank Odo and drop a few coppers in his hand for the news. "Keep a true candle burning at your toll-booth tonight if you can spare the brazier, friend, and don't buy any pale ones with a copied anvil on the base." I show him the false stub from Garl's pocket so he knows what to look for, then I head into the inn for a hot meal, a bed, and questions about whether that tinker stopped in Copper Ford's pits.

(For the count you asked after: you're carrying 14 gp 8 sp on you now — the coin in your pouch was 15 gold even, and your coppers to Odo and tonight's supper and bed came out of it. And you carry four true Vigil candles, wrapped in the temple's waxed cloth, the false stub, and Hessa's lantern freshly filled.)

Odo squints at Garl's stub in the brazier-light, turns it once, and shudders. "Copied anvil, right enough. Well — I buy my light off the chandler on the west bank, always have." He takes your coppers with a free hand, and lights his brazier up larger, as if to say he'll do his part. "Grey gloves, past my bridge, heading west. Quarry folk at Slatewick were next on that road, far as I know."

The Ferryman's Rest is low-beamed and smells of onions and river-damp, run by a broad woman named Gelda who sets a bowl of stew in front of you before you've finished asking. But she goes quiet at the tinker.

"Aye, he came. Three weeks back, sold candles up and down the pit rows, cheap as straw, and never haggled once — same as you say." She wipes her hands slowly. "And here's where you're not going to enjoy your stew, gate-guard." She leans on the bar. "Past three days, my miners have started talking about lights. Down in the low drift under the ford. Lights that walk, they say, swinging easy, like a man carrying a lantern — and swinging steady where no man can walk." She looks you full in the face. "And yesterday morning, a boy named Tam went down to check a sump with two others, and only two came up. His mother's in my kitchen right now, refusing to sit."

A spoon of stew will hold you or falling through this village will not: Greyhollow's whole story, candles first, lights after, missing men last — Copper Ford is three weeks behind the same clock, and the hand that wound it is still somewhere up the west road. But Tam went down yesterday, not three days ago. There may be time, here, that there wasn't at home.

What does Brakka do?

I put the spoon down. "Gelda, take me to Tam's mother, and then to whoever was with him. I need to know where the sump is, whether they carried the pale candles down, and if any are still in the miners' houses. I'll go down tonight with true flame, but I'll gather every false one first, and the boys' families keep them out of the pits."

Tam's mother is Mira, and she's still standing in the kitchen, thirty hours on her feet, because sitting means admitting there's nothing to stand up for. When you say you've done this before — gone down after the lights and come up with a man under one arm — something in her finally breaks the right way, and she cries into your pauldron like it's the church. She makes you take her stew. You'll carry her son out or carry her word, she says. Either is an answer.

The two miners who came up are easier to find and harder to talk to; one of them can't look you in the eye. But you've had a gate-guard's six years of watching men hold something back, and you wait them out until it comes up like a splinter. The truth: nobody ordered Tam down to any sump. They were near the old ladder-way through the low drift when knocking started up from below them — three-and-three, over and over, patient. Tam said, "That's a man, that's the code," and started down the ladder toward it. They called after him. They didn't follow. They ran for help instead, and by the time anyone had nerve enough to go back down with a dozen men and lamps, the low drift was empty and the knocking was done.

And his hands are shaking when he says it, and he means the man wrong. Three-and-three. The same signal. This tinker's stock is one pattern, working its way up the west road town by town.

The candle-gathering goes like Grayhollow taught you it would: door after door in the pit rows, and pale false-anviled stubs coming out of cupboards, pockets, children's window-sills — nearly ninety of them by the time you've done, three weeks of a village's buying, tipped into an iron pot Gelda gives you for the purpose. The foreman, a decent block named Pell, eyes the pot and says the village will melt them in his forge come morning, and swears his rows won't buy candle-stuff off any cart again.

It's half past eight in the evening, dark as a pit-head, and the Copper Ford men will follow you down the ladder-way, or stand guard at the top — Pell rounds you up a dozen and says both, but no farther than your word. You've four true Vigil candles, ten torches, Hessa's lantern, and everything you learned at Greyhollow: iron is nothing to them, small light is their lantern-lure, wide bright flame is the wall they will not cross.

The pit mouth of the low drift breathes cold under the stars. What does Brakka do?

description.text: A mining town cut into a cold mountainside, where Brakka Ironvein served six years as a temple guard. The town council has ordered the mine entrance bricked up at sunrise tomorrow.
The temple in Greyhollow where Brakka served as guard for six years. Its prior is Hessa.
The god worshipped in Greyhollow's temple; Brakka is an acolyte of his faith and carries his holy symbol.
The old dwarf who serves as prior of the Temple of the Anvil Father in Greyhollow.

The sealed-off north part of Greyhollow's mine, closed a generation ago. Three days ago three miners went down and did not return; a fourth man came up babbling about lights that walk, and died before dawn. The council bricks up the entrance at sunrise tomorrow.

Brakka went down to the workings on the evening of Day 1 and was struck senseless twice by the walker's lightning, but his heart held and he was dragged to safety by Doran; a candle stub with a copied anvil mark was found near the mine cart; the walker was driven off by torchlight at the stair's foot and waits below in the dark, as does the second pale light.
Three miners of Greyhollow who went down into the old north workings three days ago and never came back.
Last night a fourth man came up alone out of the old north workings, babbling about lights that walk, and died before dawn.
Hessa asked Brakka to go down into the old north workings before sunrise, when the council bricks up the entrance, and bring back whoever can still be brought back.
The player character: a hill dwarf fighter and acolyte of the Anvil Father.

A Greyhollow miner found alive in the old north workings behind a rubble fall, pinned by his leg, hammering the three-and-three signal. He is the last of the three missing miners still breathing down there.

Freed and rescued on the evening of Day 1 of Thaw 9th by Brakka Ironvein, who was himself struck down twice by the walker; Doran repaid it by dragging Brakka up the stair to the surface by torchlight.
One of the three missing miners. The "knockers" lured him with their too-patient tapping; taken somewhere below, per Doran's account.
One of the three missing miners. Near the shaft a small walking light came to him soft as a candle, and he went to it smiling; not seen again.

The things Doran calls the knockers and the little lights: pale, lantern-sized lights that drift and sway like a lamp in a walker's hand, down in the old north workings. False creatures of the dark; they knock the miners' code too perfectly and too patiently, and lure men close with a soft light until the men go to it smiling. Doran says Garl was taken by their tapping and Fenn by a light near the shaft. They wait patiently at the edge of the light.
A rescue at the brink: Brakka fell to 0 HP, fought the dark off with three death saves, and Doran stood over him with two torches, dragging him to the stair and up before the walker could reach him.

Doran says that in his grandfather's day miners went missing in the north workings too, and the temple sealed them and left candle offerings; the walker's light cannot pass a wide, bright flame, only iron and the anvil mark mean nothing to it. Brakka pleaded with Hessa not to let the masons brick the entrance at dawn, since Garl and Fenn are still down there.

The broken seal and descending stair at the mouth of the old north workings, just outside Greyhollow. The council will brick it up at sunrise. Brakka and Doran escaped up its stair by torchlight on the evening of Day 1.

The old sealing rite of Greyhollow's temple, recorded in the temple archive by the prior who sealed the north workings a generation ago. Tallow candles stamped with the Anvil Father's mark, struck and blessed by temple hands, set burning at the mine mouth at dusk each equinox; the true-mark flame keeps the walking lights from the mouth. The record warns that a false mark — an anvil copied by hands outside the temple — does not ward but invites: a false candle burns on its own in the dark, and the lights carry such small flames. The record also calls the walker-things 'the cold tallow' who serve something older below the third wall.

A clue from the archive: the old prior's record notes that false-mark candles were found once before, placed by miners' hands in the year of the second wall — the miners could not say where they'd gotten them, only afterward, that a peddler had come through Greyhollow before it began. The fourth miner who died may have carried such a candle down three days ago. Who sells them now is unknown.

Hessa half remembers that a tinker with a cart — no name anyone kept — came through Greyhollow a month or so back, at the winter market, selling cheap candles in lots to the miners' rows. She cannot swear it's the same trade as the old false candles, but the timing sits wrong with her. The temple pours and strikes true Vigil candles on the night before Day 2's council, Brakka helping with the work.
The heavy-set quarrymistress who heads Greyhollow's town council. Ordered the mine mouth bricked at sunrise after the missing miners.

Garl's widow, a small woman with her husband's ring on a cord. Sharp on grief and sharper on facts: she remembers the grey-gloved tinker who never haggled and always sold in lots, and watched him leave west on the high road. She told Brakka to find him, and Brakka gave his word. She kept a false-mark candle stub from Garl's coat pocket and gave it to Brakka.

A small village on the high road west of Greyhollow, half a day's walk, where the road crosses a river. First staging post on the way west. A grey-gloved tinker passed through here heading west about three weeks before the events at the mine, per Duff at the toll post.

The toll-keeper at the bridge at Copper Ford, a chatty old man with a brazier. Three weeks back he waved through a grey-gloved tinker with a hand-cart full of candles heading west; the man paid with old coin and never haggled. Odo recalls he asked about villages with mines.
A quarry-town district further west along the high road beyond Copper Ford, all dug into the hills; Odo told the tinker the road's mined villages, and the tinker nodded like a man ticking a list.

The broad, salty innkeeper of the Ferryman's Rest at Copper Ford. She remembers the grey-gloved tinker selling cheap candles in the mining rows about three weeks back, and says the pits below the ford have gone wrong in the last days: lights walking underground, and one young miner, Tam, missing since yesterday.
The inn at Copper Ford, its fire, food, and beds. Kept by Gelda.

In the last days Copper Ford's pits have gone the way of Greyhollow's: miners speaking of lights that walk in the lower drifts, three weeks after a grey-gloved tinker sold cheap candles all down the mining rows. A young miner named Tam went down yesterday and has not come up.

The drift where Tam vanished is the low drift under the river ford, an old sump level. Under Brakka's Insight the two miners who came up confessed: knocking sounded from below — three-and-three, perfect — and Tam said "that's a man" and climbed down a ladder toward it while they fled for help.

A young miner of Copper Ford who went down to check a sump in the low drift under the ford the morning of Day 1; his two companions came up and he did not. Missing, and perhaps alive, if the Greyhollow pattern holds.

Tam's mother, a kitchen-woman at the Ferryman's Rest, refusing to sit since her son went down the morning before Brakka's arrival. Brakka promised to bring back Tam, or word of him, before he moves on.

sheet.name: Brakka Ironvein
sheet.opening: Brakka Ironvein served six years as a guard at the Temple of the Anvil Father in Greyhollow, a mining town cut into a cold mountainside. Three days ago three miners went down into the old north workings, which were sealed a generation ago, and none came back. features: Darkvision: You have superior vision in dark and dim conditions. You can see in dim light within 60 feet of you as if it were bright light, and in darkness as if it were dim light. You cannot discern color in darkness, only shades of gray.
Dwarven Resilience: You have advantage on saving throws against poison, and you have resistance against poison damage.

Stonecunning: Whenever you make an Intelligence (History) check related to the origin of stonework, you are considered proficient in the History skill and add double your proficiency bonus to the check, instead of your normal proficiency bonus.
Dwarven Combat Training: You have proficiency with the battleaxe, handaxe, light hammer, and warhammer.
Tool Proficiency: You gain proficiency with the artisan's tools of your choice: smith's tools, brewer's supplies, or mason's tools.
Dwarven Toughness: Your hit point maximum increases by 1, and it increases by 1 every time you gain a level.

Fighting Style: You adopt a particular style of fighting as your specialty. Choose one of the following options. You can't take a Fighting Style option more than once, even if you later get to choose again. CHOSEN: Fighting Style: Dueling.

Second Wind: You have a limited well of stamina that you can draw on to protect yourself from harm. On your turn, you can use a bonus action to regain hit points equal to 1d10 + your fighter level. Once you use this feature, you must finish a short or long rest before you can use it again.
Fighting Style: Dueling: When you are wielding a melee weapon in one hand and no other weapons, you gain a +2 bonus to damage rolls with that weapon.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

features: Darkvision: You have superior vision in dark and dim conditions. You can see in dim light within 60 feet of you as if it were bright light, and in darkness as if it were dim light. You cannot discern color in darkness, only shades of gray.
Dwarven Resilience: You have advantage on saving throws against poison, and you have resistance against poison damage.

Stonecunning: Whenever you make an Intelligence (History) check related to the origin of stonework, you are considered proficient in the History skill and add double your proficiency bonus to the check, instead of your normal proficiency bonus.
Dwarven Combat Training: You have proficiency with the battleaxe, handaxe, light hammer, and warhammer.
Tool Proficiency: You gain proficiency with the artisan's tools of your choice: smith's tools, brewer's supplies, or mason's tools.
Dwarven Toughness: Your hit point maximum increases by 1, and it increases by 1 every time you gain a level.

Fighting Style: You adopt a particular style of fighting as your specialty. Choose one of the following options. You can't take a Fighting Style option more than once, even if you later get to choose again. CHOSEN: Fighting Style: Dueling.

Second Wind: You have a limited well of stamina that you can draw on to protect yourself from harm. On your turn, you can use a bonus action to regain hit points equal to 1d10 + your fighter level. Once you use this feature, you must finish a short or long rest before you can use it again.
Fighting Style: Dueling: When you are wielding a melee weapon in one hand and no other weapons, you gain a +2 bonus to damage rolls with that weapon.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.

sheet.name: Brakka Ironvein
sheet.opening: Brakka Ironvein served six years as a guard at the Temple of the Anvil Father in Greyhollow, a mining town cut into a cold mountainside. Three days ago three miners went down into the old north workings, which were sealed a generation ago, and none came back. Last night a fourth man came up out of the dark alone, babbling about lights that walk, then died before dawn. The town council will brick up the mine entrance at sunrise tomorrow, missing miners or not. The temple's prior, an old dwarf named Hessa, has asked Brakka to go down before then and bring back whoever can still be brought back. It is late afternoon, and Brakka stands at the mine mouth with a lantern borrowed from the temple.

input.text:
Greyhollow is a mean little town with a rich vein under it: houses of dark stone huddled against a mountainside where winter lingers long past its season. The Anvil Father — god of forgework, patience, and iron that holds — has a temple here, and for six years you, Brakka Ironvein, kept its gate. Not the loftiest calling for a dwarf of the Ironveins, but steady, and the prior trusted you.

Three days ago, three miners pried open the old north workings — sealed a generation back, before your time — and went down. None came up. Last night a fourth man crawled out alone, raving about lights that walk in the dark, and died before dawn with cold in his bones. The council has had enough: at sunrise, masons brick the entrance shut, souls inside or no souls at all.

Hessa, the temple's prior, put her old hand on your shoulder this morning. "Bring back whoever can still be brought back," she said, and lent you a hooded lantern. That is all the send-off you got.

Now it is late afternoon, the light going grey and cold, and you stand at the mine mouth. The new timber around the old seal is splintered where the miners broke through, and beyond it the shaft breathes out cold air that smells of wet stone and something faintly wrong underneath, like snuffed candles. Your lantern is unlit at your hip. The descent ahead is dark, and sunrise is your deadline.

What does Brakka do?

input.text:
The lantern catches on the first try, its flame steadying behind smudged glass, half-shielded by the hood. You set it between your boots while you work: buckles of the shield strap cinched, the longsword drawn a hand's width and slid back — loose, the way you like it. Crossbow slung. Rope on your hip. All as it should be.

The ground at the entrance is another matter. The cold has baked the trampled mud into a hard crust, and between that, your own six years of tramping gate duty, and the dark closing in, you can make little of it. You can see that boots went in — that much is obvious from the splintered seal — but how many, how fast, whether they came back out at any point, whether anything followed the fourth man up... the earth won't say. You're no tracker.

One thing does catch the lantern light, tucked against the inside of the new timber where someone must have set it down and never picked it up: a short-handled miner's pick, and beside it a horn whistle on a thong, the kind the miners carry to signal along the levels.

Cold air moves past your face, up out of the shaft, steady as breathing. Somewhere below, faint, you think you hear stone knock against stone — once, twice — like a hammer on the Anvil Father's forge. Or like water. Or like nothing.

Beyond the broken seal, a rough stair of cut steps descends into the dark, slick with old damp.

Your lantern will burn about six hours on its oil. It's near a quarter to six in the evening; sunrise is your wall.

What does Brakka do?

input.text:
You slip the horn whistle over your neck beside the holy symbol and take up the lantern.

The first steps are the worst for slip, but dwarves are born to stone, and you take them slow, boot-heel first. The stair runs down deeper than any worked level you know of in Greyhollow — fifty steps, then a turn in the rock, then fifty more, the lantern's hooded beam swinging shadows across walls scored with pick-marks a generation old.

Halfway down, you stop. And this time you hear it, truly hear it: not water, not loose rock. It's knocking — metal on stone, coming up from below and to the east. And it's in a pattern. Three knocks, a pause, then three more. Three-and-three, over and over, patient as a heartbeat.

You know that pattern. Every tunnel-child of Greyhollow knows the miners' tapping code. Three-and-three is the oldest signal in it: alive, alive, still alive. Someone down there is awake, and hammering for anyone who might hear.

That's more than you hoped for an hour ago. But a cold thought follows it: whoever is knocking never knocked when the fourth man climbed out past them — or he did, and the man who died didn't care to answer.

At the stair's foot the passage opens onto a landing where the mud is churned by many boots — too jumbled for you to count sets or say which way any man walked, and you are no tracker. The best you can say is that bodies went both ways through here, and one line of prints looks dragged and stumbling, as if made by a man barely walking. Between you and the knocking, a tunnel runs east, and the lantern light catches an old mine cart half off its rails, a rake of rusted tools, and a timber post chalked with a paw-shaped smear of old paint. Past the cart, something pale and small lies on the floor of the tunnel.

What does Brakka do?

input.text:
You leave the whistle hanging silent and move east, unhurried, keeping your weight on your boot heels. The tunnel swallows the last daylight behind you; the lantern's shielded beam is your whole world now.

You stop two paces short of the pale thing. It lies near the cart's ruined wheel, and you lean the lantern low over it without going closer.

It's a candle. A stub of pale tallow, no longer than your thumb, burned hollow at the wick, set upright on the stone as carefully as if someone placed it there. The flame is long gone. What keeps the small hairs up on your neck is the spiral of soot around the stub — the wax burned while standing here, down near floor level, far out of anyone's reach of the entrance, with no holder, no sconce, no smear of drips on the wall above it. A candle that simply sat on bare rock and burned itself down. Carved into its base, faint and worn, is a little struck anvil — maker's mark or god's sign, you can't say. The Anvil Father's mark would be warm to your touch, temple work being yours. This one isn't. This one feels like something copied from his sign by someone who'd only had it described.

You kneel there, hurry-thumping heart and steady hand. The knocking goes on eastward, three-and-three, patient as water — and you notice that when your boots scuffed the gravel by the cart, the knocking stopped a moment after, listening, going still as stone before it started again. Whatever hammers will have heard you coming. It waits for an answer, and waits — three and three, still alive. Honest men answer that call, sooner or later. But you've been a gate-guard long enough to know that other things knock, too.

Down the tunnel east, the lantern shows maybe forty feet before the dark swallows it, timber crosses marching away like ribs.

What does Brakka do?

input.text:
You press the anvil to your lips and murmur the short prayer — iron that holds, Father, hold me — and go on with the lantern shuttered to a knife of light.

It's slow going, and the chain mail works against you, but you move the way you learned on night gate: boot finding stone before weight follows, breath low, no metal allowed to touch metal. Whatever listens down here, you'll not give it your footsteps cheap.

The knocking draws you east, then bends north at a junction where the timber is older and splintered — and there, thirty paces on, a side gallery mouths open, half-choked with a fall of rubble. The knocking comes from behind the fall. As your light gropes up to it, the hammering stutters and stops. A cough. Then a voice, cracked and small, from between two boulders where a gap shows dark: "Is someone there? By the Father, quickly — the candle — don't let them light me —"

Through the gap, lanternlight on a smutched face and one terrified eye. A living miner, sitting wedged in the rubble with one leg pinned under a slab, a pick-head in his fist — the hammer you heard. He's been down here three days on cold drip-water and whatever chalk he could scrape off the wall. He whispers his name like a prayer: Doran.

"Don't answer them," he breathes, eyes rolling toward the main tunnel behind you. "They knock back. They knock perfect, like a man, but they knock too patient. That's how they got Garl. And Fenn near the shaft — a little light took him, soft as a candle coming, and he went to it smiling."

Far down the main tunnel, south and behind you, at the very edge of the shuttered lantern's reach — two small pale lights hang in the black. Not lanterns. They sway gently, side to side, the way a lamp swings in a walker's hand. They are not coming closer. They are waiting, patient as you were told.

Doran's hand gropes through the gap for you, and beyond, the rubble fall rises halfway to the ceiling, sloped and shifty-looking, three tons of bad masonry between your hands and his.

What does Brakka do?

input.text:
You grip Doran's hand through the gap — his fingers are ice-cold and shaking, but they close on yours like a smith's vice. "Brakka," he whispers back, half-laughing with relief, "the Anvil Father sends me a gate-guard."

You close the lantern's shutter entirely, and darkness folds down over the both of you like a lid. Somewhere far south, the pale lights still hang. Doubling your night-sight in this velvet black, you can just make them out — unchanged, patient.

"Keep it dark," Doran breathes, "they come to light when it's small. A candle, a guttering torch — small light draws 'em, like moths if moths hunted men. Garl's lamp died and they came for him within the hour. And when I threw Fenn a burning rag off a stick, they swung off wide around its flare — bright light they'll skirt, and small light they'll stalk toward."

"Your iron and your sign?" A bitter, cracked whisper. "Fenn had the anvil burned into his pick-haft, same as mine. Didn't slow them. They're not wolves to be fought, Brakka. They knock like men and they light like candles and they wait. They waited three days for me. They want me to walk to them."

In the blackness, the pale lights shift for the first time — they've drifted a slow, lazy ten feet closer along the main tunnel, in perfect silence, and stopped again. They're at the edge of where your own darkness ends, patient as you were told, waiting for the moment the small light they love comes back.

You know darkness yourself — sixty feet of it, grey but seeing, yours without any flame at all.

What does Brakka do?

RULE Combat Step by Step:
1.  **Determine surprise.** The GM determines whether anyone involved in the combat encounter is surprised.
2.  **Establish positions.** The GM decides where all the characters and monsters are located. Given the adventurers' marching order or their stated positions in the room or other location, the GM figures out where the adversaries are/how far away and in what direction.
3.  **Roll initiative.** Everyone involved in the combat encounter rolls initiative, determining the order of combatants' turns.
4.  **Take turns.** Each participant in the battle takes a turn in initiative order.
5.  **Begin the next round.** When everyone involved in the combat has had a turn, the round ends. Repeat step 4 until the fighting stops.

The rules sections these steps name, in full:

RULE Surprise:
A band of adventurers sneaks up on a bandit camp, springing from the trees to attack them. A gelatinous cube glides down a dungeon passage, unnoticed by the adventurers until the cube engulfs one of them. In these situations, one side of the battle gains surprise over the other.

The GM determines who might be surprised. If neither side tries to be stealthy, they automatically notice each other. Otherwise, the GM compares the Dexterity (Stealth) checks of anyone hiding with the passive Wisdom (Perception) score of each creature on the opposing side. Any character or monster that doesn't notice a threat is surprised at the start of the encounter.

If you're surprised, you can't move or take an action on your first turn of the combat, and you can't take a reaction until that turn ends. A member of a group can be surprised even if the other members aren't.

RULE The Order of Combat:
A typical combat encounter is a clash between two sides, a flurry of weapon swings, feints, parries, footwork, and spellcasting. The game organizes the chaos of combat into a cycle of rounds and turns. A **round** represents about 6 seconds in the game world. During a round, each participant in a battle takes a **turn**. The order of turns is determined at the beginning of a combat encounter, when everyone rolls initiative. Once everyone has taken a turn, the fight continues to the next round if neither side has defeated the other.

Sections inside it (look each up): Combat Step by Step, Surprise, Initiative, Your Turn, Reactions

RULE Initiative:
Initiative determines the order of turns during combat. When combat starts, every participant makes a Dexterity check to determine their place in the initiative order. The GM makes one roll for an entire group of identical creatures, so each member of the group acts at the same time.

The GM ranks the combatants in order from the one with the highest Dexterity check total to the one with the lowest. This is the order (called the initiative order) in which they act during each round. The initiative order remains the same from round to round.

If a tie occurs, the GM decides the order among tied GM-controlled creatures, and the players decide the order among their tied characters. The GM can decide the order if the tie is between a monster and a player character. The light closes on you fast — like a lamp swinging in a sprinting man's hand — and stops dead a foot from your shield-face, swelling from candle-glow to bonfire-bright in the space of a heartbeat. For half a blink, and only that, you can see inside it: a little curling blue-white shape, like a knot of pale smoke, hovering.

Then it strikes. Lightning leaps the small gap and slams through your shield arm and armor both, every joint in your body locking at once, your teeth buzzing. Your chain mail rings like a struck bell. You've taken worse knocks from the forge-gang's brawls, but not many — the pain sits in your bones and stays. You're standing, barely rocked, at 5 of your full strength out of 14; your breath is ragged.

The walker hangs there at the rim of your shield, bright and patient, like a smith waiting to see if the iron's done.

Behind you, Doran keeps flat behind the rubble as you ordered, but his voice carries a hiss of pure terror across the gap: "When it swells bright, it's striking! Bright means strike — and there's two of them, remember! TWO!"

Your turn, Brakka.

The torch catches — a guttering, resinous roar of real flame — and you sweep it at the walker as you turn to run.

You never make a step. Iron doesn't hurt the thing, but lightning doesn't care about armor either: as you pivot away it strikes you in the back of the shoulder, and every muscle you own lets go at once. input.text:
You are not there for most of it, Brakka. You'll have it from Doran's mouth later, hoarse and wondering, and this is how he'll tell it:

How he planted one torch upright in a crack of the rubble so the dark couldn't sneak in behind you, and hauled you by the collar, one fist of fire sweeping, fifteen feet at a time, while the walker circled at the rim of the light like a wolf pacing a fire ring. How he heard the water of your breathing change as he dragged you over the landing stones, and knew you were holding on. How at the stair's foot he rammed both torches together into one blazing bloom and swung you over his shoulder — a dwarf in chain mail, heavier than any ore-cart — and climbed, one step at a time, a hundred wet steps of the ancestors, weeping and swearing in the same breath, while the pale light swelled below him in a fury it could not spend.

And how, at the top, he set you down on cold grass under real stars, took the horn whistle from around your neck, and blew three-and-three into the night until his lungs tore — alive, alive, still alive — while behind the two of you, out of the broken seal, the mine breathed its cold, and somewhere down in it a light hung patient, and another one hung farther off, waiting for easier men.

They came — townsfolk, masons, Hessa herself with her robes kilted up and a lantern in her fist, running through the dusk on the strength of that whistle. You'll wake to her voice, near midnight, in a bed under the temple's roof, with every ache in your body speaking at once but your heart still beating — you pulled through the night on your own iron, Brakka, waking at last with a thread of your strength back. Doran is on the next cot, swaddled and fed, telling anyone who'll listen that the gate-guard came down and stood between him and the dark.

For that — going down before sunrise and bringing back the one soul that could be brought back — the night pays you its dues (225 XP toward your next level; 225 of 300).

But morning is coming, and this is what you know before any councilman does: the mine mouth is to be bricked at sunrise regardless, with Brakka in it or not — and down in the dark, the walking lights are still waiting, and Garl and Fenn are down there still. They knocked like men, once. Perfect. Too patient.

What does Brakka do, waking in the temple infirmary near midnight?

input.text:
You wake to lamplight and a roof-beam you know — the temple infirmary — and every bone you own objects as you sit up. Your strength is a thread, but your own: one point of your fourteen, and real sleep somewhere ahead of you.

Hessa is in the chair beside your cot, prayer book open on her knees, and hasn't left it, they say. She hears you out — the walker, the lightning, the treadmill of dark — without one flicker of surprise, which surprises you.

"So it was them," she says at last, very quietly. "I had a whole homily prepared to convince you not to go down, and the Father spared me the waste." She looks at you a long moment. "The council will brick it at dawn either way, Brakka; they're frightened men, and frightened men like finished walls. But hear this from me, as one of the temple: iron and the anvil mark mean nothing to those things — you've the bruises to prove it — but there is old work beneath that seal. In Doran's grandfather's day, miners went down the north workings and didn't come up, and the temple of that generation didn't fight what they found. The prior of those days sealed the workings with prayer and left candle offerings at the mouth — a rite even I only half remember. Whatever walked then was bottled, not slain. Your friend with the torch bought back its patience, and that's the whole of our victory today."

At your question, Doran drags himself onto one elbow from the next cot, grey-faced but sharp-eyed. "Testify? Aye, if you hold my arm up in front of me." His voice steadies as an idea takes him. "Give me one hour at that council with a torch in my fist and they'll not lay one brick till they've heard every cracked word from me. But they like walls, the council." He looks sideways at you, then says the thing that's been sitting behind his eyes:

"Brakka. My grandfather sealed that drift. But he told me once, drunk and honest: 'The wall's the third wall down there. The first two our fathers built, and the Lights came through both.' Three walls. That's what he said. There's something down beneath the north workings that even the lights answer to."

Hessa stands. "Rest tonight, both of you, or I'll have the cots nailed shut. Before dawn, if anyone moves that council, it'll be these three: Doran's tongue, my prior's oath, or your hands, gate-guard. Sleep and choose."

It is near ten o'clock at night. Sunrise is roughly nine hours off. Fire, walls old and new, and something below that even the lights answer to. What does Brakka do?

input.text:
Hessa takes you down the archive stair herself, lamplight on stone shelves, and you tell her of the candle on your way — the pale stub, the copied anvil, burned hollow standing on bare rock with no hand near it. She stops on the stair at that, and her face does flicker now.

"Then the seal's been nursed at," she says. "Someone set the door open a crack."

The search is long — you are no scholar, and your head still rings — but dwarves read stone-quiet rooms well, and somewhere past midnight your hand finds what the temple's own memory lost: the prior's record of the sealing, in her own crabbed hand. The rite is called the Vigil of Bottled Dark. Tallow candles stamped with the anvil, the mark struck and blessed by temple hands — temple hands, it says twice, underscored — set burning at the mouth at dusk, every equinox, one generation of quiet keeping on another. The ward was never the wall. The ward was the true flame.

And then the page that makes the ward your candle at the mine: a warning, in走了 the same crabbed hand. That a false mark — an anvil copied by hands outside the temple — does not ward. It invites. Such candles are found burning on bare stone in the dark, unwitnessed, small flames the lights carry in front of them like lanterns held out. And beneath the warning, a note: false-mark candles were found once before, in the workings, in the year of the second wall. The miners who'd carried them down could not say who'd taught them the making — only that a peddler had come through Greyhollow shortly before men began going down and not coming up. The page calls what serves below the third wall nothing but a name half-ashamed of itself: the cold tallow.

Hessa reads the page twice, then sits down on the archive stair like her knees have been unhinged. "The equinox rites were kept in my grandmother's time," she says slowly. "I thought them a dead grandmother's superstition. In mine, the archive says, they were missed — twice. And someone has been selling false candles to our miners." Her jaw sets like cooling steel. "There is tallow in this temple, and there is a true anvil-seal stamp in my own keeping, and I am no, no — I *am* the prior of this house. If the council wants a wall at dawn, then they'll get a warded wall, by the Father, with true flame at its mouth, or I'll know the reason."

Doran is already asleep on his cot when you pass through, one arm hung down toward the floor. Near half past midnight now. Sunrise, the council, the masons, Doran's testimony, a peddler somewhere in Greyhollow's memory — and perhaps six hours of sleep, or fewer. What does Brakka do?

The miners who'd carried them down could not say who'd taught them the making — only that a peddler had come through Greyhollow shortly before men began going down and not coming up. The page calls what waits below the third wall nothing but a name half-ashamed of itself: the cold tallow.

Hessa reads the page twice, then sits down on the archive stair like her knees have been unhinged. "The equinox rites were kept in my grandmother's time," she says slowly. "I thought them a dead grandmother's superstition. In mine, the archive says, they were missed — twice. And someone has been selling false candles to our miners." Her jaw sets like cooling steel. "There is tallow in this temple, and there is a true anvil-seal stamp in my own keeping. If the council wants a wall at dawn, then they'll get a warded wall, by the Father, with true flame at its mouth, or I'll know the reason."

Doran is already asleep on his cot when you pass through, one arm hung down toward the floor. It is near half past midnight. Sunrise, the council, the masons, Doran's testimony, a peddler somewhere in Greyhollow's memory — and perhaps six hours of sleep, or fewer. What does Brakka do?

input.text:
The back room of the temple smells of rendered fat and herbs until dawn comes up grey. Hessa strikes the anvil-seal into each candle's base herself — temple hands, she says again, like a smith saying good iron — while you stir the tallow, pour the molds, and set each finished stub on waxed cloth. Twelve true candles before the birds start. Your own hands know the work; turns out a gate-guard who six years watched the forge-priests at their bench remembers more than he thought. You don't sleep, and by the last hour your body's telling you so — you are still at a thread of your strength, and your breath is long, unwound iron. (You'll feel this until you truly rest, Brakka.)

On the peddler, she can give you this much, stirring beside you: a tinker with a cart — no name anyone kept — came through Greyhollow a month or so back, round the winter market, selling cheap candles in lots to the miners' rows. "Cheap tallow, pale wax, no temple stamp on any of them, and the miners bought them by the dozen because winter nights are long." She can't swear it's the trade the old prior wrote of. But she says the timing sits with her like a bad tooth.

At first light you carry the crate to the mine mouth together, Doran hobbling at your side wrapped in the temple's grey, and the mountain shows you what the council means by finished walls: two masons and a handcart of bricks already waiting, breath steaming, and behind them half of Greyhollow — the council in their cloaks, miners' families, children on shoulders. Cold morning fog lies in the cut like milk.

The council head — a heavy woman named Brama, quarrymistress — looks from Hessa to the crate of candles to the wall of the hill. "Prior," she says carefully, "the town slept badly. Say what you've come to say."

It's near half five in the morning. The crowd is listening, Doran is squaring his shoulders to speak, and the sun is climbing.

What does Brakka do?
